div.head: Iudex Iudex 1
div.ab: Omnis iudex iustus misericordiam et iudicium libret in omnibus, ut inprimis per rectam scientiam dicat emendationem secundum culpam et eam tamen admensuret propter indulgentiam.

Ælc man, þe riht demeð, he hæfð wæga on handa; ⁊ on ægðere sceale he byrþ rihtwisnesse ⁊ mildheortnesse: ærest for ðære rihtwisnesse he gereceð ðæs gyltes bote ⁊ þonne for ðære mildheortnesse he gemetegað þære scylde wíte.

Every man who judges justly holds a balance in his hand: on each scale he carries justice and mercy: first, for the sake of justice he decides the punishment for the guilty, and then for the sake of mercy he moderates the pain of the penalty.

Jedermann, der richtigen Spruch ertheilt, der hat Wagschalen in der Hand; und in je einer Schale trägt er Gerechtigkeit und Barmherzigkeit: zuerst bestimmt er infolge der Gerechtigkeit Busse für die Verschuldung, und alsdann um der Barmherzigkeit willen ermässigt er die Strafe für die Schuld.

Everyone who gives a right judgment holds scales in his hand; and in each scale he carries justice and mercy: first, by reason of justice, he fixes the compensation for the offence, and then, for mercy's sake, he moderates the penalty for the guilt.
div.note: The Latin is the Quadripartitus; Liebermann's Old English is from G (Cotton Nero A I, f. 48, after Romscot, same hand c. 1060). Liebermann dates Iudex c. 980–c. 1050; it draws on Isidore, Sententiae III 52–54 (here 52.4). From 8 on the Quadripartitus probably used the source of the OE directly, Liebermann thinks.
